findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

additional_observations: No mass, midline shift or hydrocephalus
ct.impression: Non-contrast CT head: no acute intracranial abnormality. Impression: normal non-contrast CT of the head.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

output.impression: 1. Reduced FVC 2.43 L (76% predicted, 35 mL/kg). 2. Reduced MIP (-58 cmH2O) and MEP (64 cmH2O). 3. Weak cough. Mild respiratory muscle weakness; above the 20 mL/kg, -30 cmH2O and 40 cmH2O thresholds.
recommended_actions: Repeat measurement if bulbar or respiratory symptoms progress.

findings.description: 3 Hz trains of 10 stimuli; skin temperature 33 C; no anticholinesterase medication taken.
Baseline CMAP 1.8 mV; decrement 1st to 4th response 22%.
Baseline CMAP 8.9 mV; decrement 6%. After 10 s maximal contraction CMAP 9.2 mV (3% increment); no facilitation.

output.impression: 1. Decrement of 18-22% at 3 Hz in facial muscles (nasalis, orbicularis oculi). 2. No significant decrement in abductor digiti minimi; normal baseline CMAP amplitudes; no post-exercise facilitation. Findings are consistent with a postsynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission predominantly affecting facial muscles. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: Anti-MuSK antibody elevated (42 nmol/L). AChR binding and modulating antibodies not detected. TSH and free T4 within reference ranges. MuSK antibodies are found in a minority of patients with myasthenia gravis who lack AChR antibodies; clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description: 20 fiber pairs. Mean MCD 29 microseconds (reference <34). Increased jitter in 1 of 20 pairs; no blocking.
20 fiber pairs. Mean MCD 52 microseconds (reference <35). Increased jitter in 12 of 20 pairs (60%); blocking in 10% of pairs.

output.impression: 1. Normal jitter in extensor digitorum communis. 2. Increased jitter with impulse blocking in orbicularis oculi. Findings indicate a disorder of neuromuscular transmission affecting facial muscles. Clinical correlation recommended.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 76% predicted (35 mL/kg), MIP -58 and MEP 64 cmH2O, weak cough: mildly reduced, above crisis thresholds
action_criteria.label: Measure respiratory function now (FVC, MIP, MEP, cough)
action_criteria.rationale: Severe bulbar weakness needing a nasogastric tube in a 75-year-old: respiratory muscle strength must be measured at once and trended, because bulbar MG can progress to crisis (Lawn ND et al., Arch Neurol 2001).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding and modulating antibodies negative; TSH and free T4 normal
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Relapsing bulbar weakness with ophthalmoparesis raises a disorder of neuromuscular transmission; AChR binding antibody is the first-line test and TSH screens for thyroid disease (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 22% in nasalis and 18% in orbicularis oculi, 6% in ADM; normal CMAPs, no facilitation
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial muscles
action_criteria.rationale: In bulbar-predominant MG, and in MuSK MG, the decrement is often confined to facial muscles, so nasalis and orbicularis oculi must be tested as well as a limb muscle (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.label: Order MuSK antibody after a negative AChR result
action_criteria.rationale: MuSK antibody testing is indicated in every AChR-negative patient; bulbar, facial and neck-predominant weakness is the typical MuSK phenotype (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025; Evoli A et al., Neurol Sci 2019).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal jitter in extensor digitorum communis; increased jitter with 10% blocking in orbicularis oculi
action_criteria.label: Single-fiber EMG including a facial muscle
action_criteria.rationale: Single-fiber EMG of a facial muscle confirms the transmission defect where a limb study may be normal, as in MuSK MG (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; age-appropriate thymic involution; no lung mass
action_criteria.label: Order mediastinal CT with contrast
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG; thymoma is rare in MuSK MG, but the CT is obtained before the antibody result is known (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No brainstem lesion; no midbrain atrophy; reduced nigral SWI signal
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI if a brainstem or supranuclear cause remains in question
action_criteria.rationale: Downgaze restriction with axial rigidity raises progressive supranuclear palsy and a brainstem lesion; MRI shows no midbrain atrophy or brainstem lesion. Optional once the antibody and neurophysiology results are in.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interactions with the current medicines
action_criteria.label: Check his medicines against pyridostigmine
action_criteria.rationale: Levodopa-carbidopa and amlodipine have no MG-relevant interaction; optional.

action_criteria.label: Review guidance on the treatment of MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading on management; not a clinical step in the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not refer for thymectomy: no benefit is established in MuSK antibody-positive MG and the CT shows no thymoma.
Do not attribute the dysphagia and ophthalmoparesis to Parkinson disease or progressive supranuclear palsy before MuSK antibody testing and neurophysiology.
required_recommendations: Diagnose MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis with severe bulbar and oculomotor involvement (MGFA class IVb, feeding tube without intubation): relapsing fatigable dysphagia and dysarthria, ophthalmoparesis without ptosis, AChR negative, MuSK 42 nmol/L, facial decrement on RNS.

Treat the severe bulbar weakness with plasma exchange (5 exchanges over about 10 days), the preferred acute therapy in MuSK MG; IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days if plasma exchange is not available [Sanders_2016].

Start prednisone in hospital under monitoring for steroid-induced worsening, with bone protection and glucose monitoring, and plan rituximab early if the response to initial immunotherapy is unsatisfactory [Sanders_2016].
Use pyridostigmine only cautiously at low dose, if at all: MuSK MG often responds poorly and patients may show cholinergic hypersensitivity, and increased secretions worsen dysphagia.
Continue nasogastric feeding with aspiration precautions and a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment before oral intake resumes.
Repeat FVC and MIP at least daily while bulbar weakness is severe; transfer to ICU-level care if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg, MIP is weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O, or secretions pool.
Reassess the parkinsonism (levodopa response, possible coexisting Parkinson disease) once the bulbar disease is treated.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a disorder of the neuromuscular junction (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to the diagnosis of MG.
CSF has no role in MG (Jacob S et al., Pract Neurol 2025); it does not address the bulbar weakness.

accepted: MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis, bulbar-predominant, with ophthalmoplegia without ptosis

differential.key_features: Downgaze restriction, axial rigidity, frontal release signs and an astonished expression suggest it, but the bulbar weakness relapses and remits, MRI shows no midbrain atrophy, and MuSK antibodies and a facial RNS decrement are present.

differential.diagnosis: Parkinson disease as the cause of the bulbar dysfunction
differential.key_features: Asymmetric rest tremor with a modest levodopa response may reflect coexisting Parkinson disease, but it does not cause relapsing fatigable bulbar weakness or ophthalmoparesis.
Tongue weakness and a brisk masseter reflex raise it, but there are no fasciculations or wasting, the course relapses and remits over two years, and MuSK antibodies are positive.
AChR binding and modulating antibodies negative; MuSK positive.
Single lactate of 2.5 mmol/L normal on repeat, muscle biopsy without COX or SDH abnormality, relapsing course.
Relapsing-remitting fatigable deficits over two years and no brainstem lesion on MRI.

key_clinical_evidence: Two years of relapsing-remitting severe dysphagia with nasal dysarthria, tongue weakness and ophthalmoparesis without ptosis, now needing a nasogastric tube.
AChR binding and modulating antibodies negative; anti-MuSK antibody 42 nmol/L.
RNS: decrement of 22% in nasalis and 18% in orbicularis oculi with 6% in ADM; SFEMG normal in extensor digitorum and abnormal in orbicularis oculi, the facial-predominant pattern of MuSK MG.
Respiratory function mildly reduced (FVC 35 mL/kg, MIP -58, MEP 64 cmH2O) with a weak cough: above crisis thresholds, but needs trending.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows no thymoma; thymectomy is not indicated in MuSK MG.
MuSK MG responds poorly to pyridostigmine and well to plasma exchange; rituximab is an early option.
Parkinsonism (rest tremor, axial rigidity, gait freezing) may coexist and does not explain the fatigable bulbar weakness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fatigable bulbar weakness, fluctuating ophthalmoplegia, and MuSK antibody positivity are MG; Parkinson can coexist but does not explain the fatigable pattern.
red_herrings.data_point: Asymmetric rest tremor diagnosed as possible Parkinson's disease; reduced nigral signal on SWI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute bulbar dysphagia to PD progression and miss MuSK MG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The eye movement restriction is from neuromuscular transmission failure (facial decrement on RNS, MuSK antibodies), not supranuclear; the relapsing-remitting course and the absence of midbrain atrophy are against PSP or MSA.
red_herrings.data_point: Parkinsonism features (tremor, gait, masked facies) suggesting PSP or MSA
red_herrings.intended_effect: Supranuclear eye movement restriction + axial rigidity + poor levodopa response fits PSP or MSA pattern

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Repeat lactate 0.9 mmol/L and a muscle biopsy without COX or SDH abnormality argue against mitochondrial disease; MuSK antibodies establish the neuromuscular junction disorder.
red_herrings.data_point: Single elevated lactate (2.5 mmol/L) suggesting mitochondrial disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Episodic bulbar dysfunction + mildly elevated lactate raises MELAS concern

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A negative AChR antibody does not exclude MG; MuSK antibody testing in AChR-negative patients is strongly positive.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative AChR antibody on initial testing
red_herrings.intended_effect: Negative AChR antibody might suggest MG is not the diagnosis

sequence_constraints.reason: MuSK antibody testing follows a negative AChR antibody result (Jacob 2025).
AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).
Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

results.finding: Patients with MuSK antibody-positive MG often respond poorly to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and respond well to plasma exchange; rituximab should be considered as an early option when the response to initial immunotherapy is unsatisfactory. Evidence does not support thymectomy in MuSK MG.

results.finding: MuSK antibodies are found in a minority of AChR antibody-negative patients and are associated with prominent bulbar, facial and neck weakness; electrodiagnostic abnormalities may be confined to facial muscles.

myasthenia gravis.summary: Consensus guidance: MuSK MG responds poorly to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and well to plasma exchange; rituximab is an early option after an unsatisfactory response to initial immunotherapy; thymectomy is not supported. MuSK MG predominantly affects bulbar, facial and neck muscles.

No brainstem lesion; no midbrain atrophy (normal midbrain-to-pons proportion); no hot cross bun sign. No acute intracranial abnormality.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia, dysarthria, and ophthalmoplegia in an elderly man with Parkinson-like features

family_history: Father had Parkinson's disease; mother had hypertension; no family history of neuromuscular or autoimmune disease
past_medical_history: Asymmetric rest tremor (left-predominant) diagnosed as possible Parkinson's disease at age 72; levodopa response modest
Two prior hospitalizations for severe dysphagia in past 3 months

social_history.note: Retired professor; non-smoker; non-drinker; widower; lives alone with daily home aide

patient.history_present_illness:
A 75-year-old man was admitted to the neurology ward for progressive dysphagia requiring nasogastric tube placement, severe dysarthria with hypophonia and nasal speech, and ophthalmoplegia without ptosis. Over the preceding two years, he had experienced similar relapsing and remitting episodes of severe dysphagia that each resolved spontaneously over days to weeks. In the three months prior to admission, he had been hospitalized twice for severe dysphagia. During those admissions a barium swallow, neck CT and a general autoimmune screen had been normal, and his response to three days of IV methylprednisolone was inconsistent. Serum lactate was 2.5 mmol/L on one occasion and 0.9 mmol/L on repeat; anti-Hu, anti-Yo and anti-Ri antibodies were negative; a biceps muscle biopsy showed type I and II fiber atrophy without COX or SDH abnormalities.

At age 72, he had developed an asymmetric rest tremor predominantly in the left leg, followed by the right leg. Brain MRI at that time was normal, and treatment with levodopa-carbidopa produced only modest benefit. On current examination, he had masked facies with decreased blink rate, an astonished expression, and ophthalmoplegia with partial restriction of downward gaze while upward gaze was partially preserved. He had no diplopia. Bulbar examination revealed severe pharyngeal weakness with dysphagia, hypophonia, nasal speech, and marked tongue weakness. The pharyngeal reflex was normal; masseter reflex was brisk. Frontal release signs (glabellar tap, palmomental, and orbicularis oris reflexes) were present. An asymmetric rest tremor of both legs, worse on the left, was noted. Limb strength was otherwise 5/5 except for areflexia in the left upper limb (with flexor plantar responses bilaterally). Axial rigidity was present with en-bloc turning and gait freezing.
